candidates.title: RRSI: Regularized Recursive Self-Improvement of Agent Harnesses
candidates.venue: arXiv preprint (cs.LG primary, cs.AI cross-list); not yet peer-reviewed
candidates.citationVelocity: submitted 2026-09-21; announced in Tuesday 2026-09-22 batch; no citation data available
candidates.institution: Google Cloud AI Research, with Stanford University, Washington University in St. Louis, and UNC-Chapel Hill co-authors
communitySignals: public code + project page: github.com/google-research/rrsi, regularized-rsi.com
credibilityEvidence: Section 3-4 gives a complete regularization design (annealed edit-budget proposer, evidence-aware credit assignment, critic+pruner selector) plus formal problem setup (Eq. 1-4)

Table 1 reports a direct head-to-head against four prior harness-evolution baselines (Meta-Harness, HarnessX, AHE, TTHE) on the same evolve split and candidate budget, showing rank inversion out of distribution
evaluated across 8 benchmarks in 3 domains (coding: SWE-bench Verified; agentic workspace: JobBench, GDPval, APEX-Agents; engineering design: Frontier-Eng)
explicit Limitations section scoping the claim to frozen-backbone harness optimization
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: large multi-domain benchmark suite with a controlled comparison against 4 named baselines under identical budget, plus a dedicated limitations section; still bounded by the chosen evolve sets and has not been tested on substantially different agent architectures
reproducibilityEvidence: public GitHub repo (google-research/rrsi, confirmed live via GitHub API) and project website with paper details
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: the claim (existing harness-evolution methods can rank-invert out of distribution, and RRSI's regularization corrects this at a measured cost in evolve-set gain) is directly read off the reported evolve/OOD table
candidates.primaryLimitation: only addresses frozen-backbone harness-layer optimization; effectiveness depends on evolve-set quality and regularization hyperparameter choices; broader validation still needed for substantially different agent architectures and tool ecosystems
candidates.presentationReason: problem setup, regularization mechanisms, and the evolve/OOD distinction are precisely defined with explicit formulas and a clearly labeled limitations section
candidates.reason: Directly tests a currently popular technique (automated harness self-improvement) for a specific, previously under-examined failure mode (evolve-to-OOD rank inversion), backed by Google-affiliated authorship, 8-benchmark evaluation, and full public artifacts; forms the 'harness' angle of today's three-layer agent-reliability cluster.

candidates.title: Harness-Zero: Harness Distillation via Agent-as-Harness
candidates.venue: arXiv preprint (cs.AI primary, cs.CL + cs.NE secondary); not yet peer-reviewed
candidates.institution: Peking University (State Key Laboratory of General Artificial Intelligence) + Google + HKUST
credibilityEvidence: clear three-stage method (harness evolution+adaptation, agent-as-harness trajectory collection, SFT on reviewed rollouts) with formal notation for the review protocol
evaluated across 3 domains (SpreadsheetBench Verified, AppWorld, USPTO Retrosynthesis) with controlled ablations against alternative supervision sources (30% vs 3-15% for weaker ablations)
concrete before/after numbers: macro-average success 23.3% -> 44.3% after removing the specialized harness at deployment, exceeding the 41.7% obtained with the harness still attached
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: 3-domain evaluation with named ablations isolating the source of the gain; primary claim (harness gains survive harness removal) is directly measured, though generality across more harness types/domains is not yet shown
reproducibilityEvidence: no public code repository link found in the sections read (abstract, intro, method); GitHub search did not surface an official release at this round
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: the narrow claim (distilling this optimized harness's behavior into weights recovers most of its gains under the fixed target harness) is directly supported by the reported before/after and ablation numbers
candidates.primaryLimitation: no public code found this round, unlike RRSI and Jev-Mem in the same cluster; reproducibility currently rests on the paper's own reported numbers
candidates.presentationReason: the harness/target-harness/reference-harness distinction and the agent-as-harness review protocol are precisely defined with explicit equations
candidates.reason: Covers essentially the same research question as selected RRSI (agent harness self-improvement/generalization) with comparable evidence quality, but RRSI's evolve/OOD rank-inversion finding is a more novel, more broadly applicable diagnostic than Harness-Zero's distillation result, and RRSI ships full public artifacts (code + project site) while Harness-Zero's reproducibility could not be confirmed this round. Selecting both would over-concentrate today's picks on one narrow sub-topic instead of covering harness/skill/memory as three distinct angles.

candidates.title: SkillSpec: Intent-Masked Specification Reasoning for Agent Skill Correctness
candidates.venue: arXiv preprint (cs.SE primary, cs.AI secondary); not yet peer-reviewed
candidates.citationVelocity: submitted 2026-09-05, surfaced via HuggingFace Daily Papers 2026-09-22 batch; no citation data available
credibilityEvidence: Section III formalizes skill correctness as Hoare-style ExpectSpec/FactSpec conformance with an intent-mask mechanism (C1/C2 challenges explicitly addressed)
evaluated on 515 real-world skills from SkillsBench + skills.sh top-downloads (SkillsTop); 763 manually confirmed defects across 239 skills (46.4%), 61.2% sandbox-validated precision
explicit Threats-to-Validity / External Validity section discussing data-leakage risk, procedural-variation controls, and non-unique graph decomposition
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: large real-world corpus with manual defect confirmation and node-level cross-model-family analysis; authors themselves flag that skill-graph decomposition is non-unique, which bounds how far results generalize across alternative decompositions
reproducibilityEvidence: public code and defect dataset released on GitHub and HuggingFace Datasets (confirmed via web_search)
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: the claim (real-world agent skills frequently contain intent/implementation mismatches detectable via specification reasoning) is directly supported by the large manually-confirmed defect count
candidates.primaryLimitation: skill-graph decomposition is inherently non-unique; results are reported against one frozen decomposition per skill to control this, and residual false positives stem from inaccurate inferred specs or unrealistic validator-constructed edge cases
candidates.presentationReason: the Hoare-logic adaptation, intent-mask visibility levels, and evaluation methodology are precisely defined with worked examples (Fig. 2-3)
candidates.reason: First systematic quality-assurance method for the specific artifact type (SKILL.md + code) that agent frameworks are now standardizing on; large real-world corpus, full public artifacts, and a distinct sub-system angle (skill correctness) from RRSI (harness) and Jev-Mem (memory), giving today's 3 picks genuine coverage across harness/skill/memory.

candidates.title: Jev-Mem: System-One-Controlled Agentic Memory for Efficient AI Agents
candidates.venue: arXiv preprint (cs.AI primary, cs.LG secondary); not yet peer-reviewed
candidates.institution: The University of Texas at Dallas
communitySignals: public code: github.com/libingzheren/Jev-Mem (confirmed live via GitHub API)
credibilityEvidence: Section 3 gives a complete System-One/System-Two architecture (control plane, multi-relational memory plane, reasoning plane) with formal memory-state notation
direct comparison against multiple existing agentic memory baselines on LoCoMo: 0.777 LLM-as-a-Judge score (+11.0% relative), 158s construction (6.6x speedup), 0.93s query latency (-36.7%)
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: performance/efficiency numbers are complete and clearly compared against named baselines, but validated only on a single long-dialogue memory benchmark (LoCoMo); no cross-task-type validation (e.g. coding assistants, long-horizon planning) yet
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: the narrow claim (separating memory control from generative reasoning improves both accuracy and efficiency on LoCoMo) is supported by complete comparison numbers, but the paper's own scope is limited to one benchmark, bounding how strongly the 'efficiency without accuracy trade-off' narrative can be generalized
candidates.primaryLimitation: validated on a single long-dialogue memory benchmark (LoCoMo) only; no evidence yet for other agent task types
candidates.presentationReason: the System-One/System-Two division of labor and the write/read path decisions it controls are precisely enumerated with a clear architecture figure
candidates.reason: Concrete systems contribution separating 'how smart memory needs to be' from 'does every memory decision need LLM generation', with public code and clean baseline comparisons; provides the 'memory efficiency' angle distinct from RRSI (harness) and SkillSpec (skill correctness), completing today's 3-paper coverage of harness/skill/memory.
